title: How are you feeding your gameplay back into the agent?
author: Icy_Cartographer5466
selftext:
Sorry for the confusing title, let me explain. I’m making games using Claude Code and Godot. But Claude Code can’t “see” videos the way it can “see” still images. So I have it take screenshots to test/verify its changes, in addition to text-based telemetry that it’s able to review. 

One game I’m working on is a physics game and screenshots alone aren’t that informative, I really want video. So I have it record a video, down sample it to \~10fps, and put the frames into a single image like a contact sheet that the model can then review. It’s hard to say if this has improved work quality though. 

Anyone have better ideas to get more information about the game back to the agent? Obviously I’m still doing a lot of manual testing but I feel like this visual/experiential gap is currently a bottleneck for setting the agents out on more ambitious tasks.

comments.author: Intelligent-Neat9974
comments.body:
Setup a Godot MCP. You can find some online that people have. Some are paid (usually like $20) and then connect claude code to it. It would allow claude to take screenshots it wants, read the errors in godot, build scenes, read settings on bodies and more.

Sites selling a godot mcp or otherwise will almost definitely have an installation guide.

replies.author: Tokey_TheBear
replies.body:
Anyone who says that quite literally has no understanding of agentic engineering...

Like literally to the point where if you see a single person say that you should immediately dismiss anything that they say in regards to AI.

MCPs are like a different variant of a skill.

Skills are meant to give the AI custom knowledge as to how it can do special things that it natively would have to spend time understanding how to do if it didn't have any special instructions.

For example I have an MCP server setup and a skill in my local game development project. The MCP server directly hooks in to the Godot engine installed on my system and that then gives the AI the knowledge that it can launch games through this protocol and then while the game is running the AI can capture screenshots of the game engine running as well as passing in game button press inputs through the MCP server.

There's quite literally no logical reason whatsoever why I would gain any benefit from getting rid of the godot MCP that I have setup juet because I am now using Fable or Sol

replies.author: Interesting-Yam23
replies.body: I don’t mind what works for people, but I’ve personally had success just writing a few scripts to let my agents interact with the engine without a big mcp. They can launch the game headlessly or with the renderer just fine without an mcp. They can also dump live scenes while the game is running. Not sure exactly what an mcp gives that a few scrips and some good guidance in agents.md can’t

replies.author: Level-Physics-1730
replies.body: this guy knows ball. if you're on godot you don't need an MCP at all. just give your agent the path to the engine EXE and let it make harnesses/auto screenshot/do whatever it can control the entire engine and game without an MCP.

replies.author: Tokey_TheBear
replies.body:
Can you explain what the benefit is? I didnt get a chance to see the other persons comment before it was deleted. 

From my understanding the MCP server is like a plugin where it contains multiple different tools and skills that the AI has access to. 

Those tools let the AI control / interact with the game efficiently.

If the AI doesnt have any extra knowledge on how to do this, then instead of spending lets say: 100 tokens executing a command that it already knows will work, it will instead have to spend the tokens to create these new extra scripts / add the functionality to your workspace for it to then do all of the things you want (that the MCP already has). 

  
If you are saying instead that you prefer the route of it having the least amount of context taken up, then you could have the AI do a one time operation to create local skills to only do the actions you need it to and nothing else. 

  
So the trade off is that you have to spend that extra time but you will have less context bloat. 

  
Am I missing something?

replies.author: Level-Physics-1730
replies.body: godot is a special case for AI game development, it's essentially AI native and the developers never made it as that. all your game's scenes are text files on your computer, the frontier AI models are trained on the format, they understand it natively. all your game scripts? text files on your PC. all your game project's godot settings? text files on the computer. AI wants to run gdscript to test something, or run your game automatically? it can just open the godot editor EXE (if you give it the path) and it can do compile checks, script exec, headless game runs, everything. godot is essentially an AI native game engine, this is why it doesn't need an MCP. unity and others need MCP because a lot of their day to day functionality is hidden in random UI, godot doesn't have that issue.

replies.author: Charming_You_25
replies.body: It’s true, mcps are dead. Long live cli tools

comments.author: BoredzzzGame
comments.body: Have Claude build a dev tool for you so you can tweak some of the physics settings in real time. This way, you understand how tweaking the values affects the physics. Have it add a copy values button to the dev tool so when you have settings that you’re happy with, Claude can apply them.

comments.author: MindlessAd4611
comments.body: I created a filmstrip util function per module (FX animation, char movement, etc), and all of my skills for implementing these modules have a note about how to use it to validate their changes, so the agent just calls the utils and reviews it visually. The utils just load up the game in isolation, zoom in to coordinates and send key events based on cli flags.. something like “—x 20 —y 20 —zoom 50 —Key C —duration 5000” for example, and it take snapshots from key press for duration, slaps it together in one png and saves to disk for review

comments.author: Will_X_Intent
comments.body: Those screenshot are going to devour tokens.  You need to use your eyes and describe to the AI what you see

comments.author: Agreeable-Safety-360
comments.body: I have my own engine I had it make, It can create a seperate instance me and the AI can work together in, in  real time, and confirm any changes before they get pushed over to my main version.  Due to this setup I can move anything around, and codex will directly see it and fully understand what's going on. I can also make annotations, pins, hand scribbles, along with a built in chatbox so I don't have to actually alt tab back over when working.

comments.author: Derreus
comments.body: Gemini pro can process videos. I’ve sent it 15-20 second videos and it gathers the context. I haven’t tried longer videos, but I’m sure you could upload in stages stating you will upload X amount of videos before discussing the feature you’re looking to fix.

comments.author: FrozenFirebat
comments.body:
I created an MCP in my game, itself, on debug configurations. The game opens a connection on localhost, and I have an API exposed that I use in an in game command console that exposes pretty much every feature and I allow the network to ride those commands. I even have a ring buffer of every important event buffer message in the game, so I or the Agent can dump a complete log of the last 10 seconds of gameplay. Sometimes when tuning, I even have the Agent take consecutive dumps of gameplay data and then analyze what works and what was underutilized.

Tools engineer by trade, so I'm trying to make a game and end up building everything but a game.

comments.author: OldManActual
comments.body: For my iOS game Claude suggested creating development code that records gameplay and exports a .csv on close. Claude has the whole session to the millisecond, no screen caps required, no tokens spent on the monitoring. This has been instrumental in squashing many bugs.
